name: netwatch
title: An internet outage logger
pitch: Your connection drops, and your internet provider says everything is fine. This program checks the connection every 30 seconds and logs every outage with its time and length. After a month, you have proof.

steps.do: Create the project with `cargo new netwatch`, and check once if the internet answers: open a TCP connection to a well-known server (for example 1.1.1.1 on port 53) with a timeout.
steps.done: the program prints "online", and "offline" when you turn off your Wi-Fi.
steps.hint: `TcpStream::connect_timeout` from std::net, with a `SocketAddr` and a `Duration` of 2 seconds.
steps.why: A TCP connection that opens proves the whole path works: your Wi-Fi, your router, your provider. The timeout stops the program from waiting forever when it doesn't.

steps.do: Check every 30 seconds, in a loop.
steps.done: the status prints again and again, and changes when you unplug.
steps.why: A monitor is a loop that never ends. Test it with a short delay: waiting 30 seconds per try is slow debugging.

steps.do: Print only the changes: "offline at 14:02", "back at 14:05".
steps.done: nothing prints while the status stays the same.
steps.hint: Keep the previous status in a variable, and compare.
steps.why: Remembering the last state and reacting to changes is called edge detection. It turns a flood of checks into a few useful events.

steps.do: Add the date and time with the chrono crate, and the length of each outage.
steps.done: "back at 14:05, offline for 3 min" is printed.
steps.hint: `chrono::Local::now()` for the time; subtract two times to get a duration.
steps.why: Time is harder than it looks (time zones, clock changes). A crate like chrono gets it right for you.

steps.do: Check two or three servers, and call it an outage only when all of them fail.
steps.done: a wrong address in the list doesn't count as an outage.
steps.hint: Put the addresses in a Vec, and use `.iter().any(…)` to know if at least one answered.
steps.why: One server can be down on its own. Asking several avoids false alarms, the same reason alarms have more than one sensor.

steps.do: Save each outage to a CSV file.
steps.done: the outages are still there after restarting the program.
steps.hint: `OpenOptions::new().append(true).create(true)` opens the file to add lines to its end.
steps.why: Append-only files are simple and safe: an outage written is never lost, even if the program stops right after.

steps.do: Handle errors without unwrap: a log file you can't write, a bad server address.
steps.done: each problem prints a clear message.
steps.hint: `match` on the Result, or `?` in a function that returns a Result, and `eprintln!` for messages.
steps.why: A program meant to run for weeks must not panic on the first problem. Decide which errors stop it and which ones it can live with.

steps.do: Add `netwatch report`: the number of outages, the total time offline and the longest one, per day and per month.
steps.done: the report matches the CSV file.
steps.hint: Read the CSV back, group by date with a HashMap or BTreeMap (it keeps keys sorted).
steps.why: The log is the raw data; the report is the answer. Keeping them apart means you can change the report without losing anything.

steps.do: Run the checks in a thread, so the program can check and write the report at the same time.
steps.done: the checks go on while the report is written.
steps.hint: `std::thread::spawn`, and a channel (`std::sync::mpsc`) to send outages from the checking thread.
steps.why: Rust checks at compile time that threads don't share data in unsafe ways. Channels are the simplest safe way to make them talk.

steps.do: Run it all the time, as a systemd user service or at startup.
steps.done: it logs outages after a reboot without you starting it.
steps.hint: A unit file in ~/.config/systemd/user/, then `systemctl --user enable --now netwatch`.
steps.why: A monitor you have to start yourself will be off on the day it matters. Services start with the machine.

steps.do: Optional: measure the latency too, and log the slow periods, not only the outages.
steps.done: the report shows the slowest hours.
steps.why: Slow is often worse than down, because people wait instead of reporting it. Now you can show both.
